title: Die Zahlen sehen schlecht aus  (The Numbers Look Bad)

segments.t: Sitting across from Thorsten in the branch office, Beyza opens the store ledger and gets straight to the point: the numbers do not look good. Thorsten stalls with nervous questions until he gives up and calls deputy manager Pina over the intercom. Listen to the German exchange first.
So, schön, dass du da bist!
Die Zahlen sehen ja nicht so gut aus, oder?
Wie meinst du das jetzt?
Wie meine ich das? Also, die Zahlen sehen nicht so gut aus.
Ja, aber was heißt das genau?
Was heißt das wohl? Die Zahlen sind einfach schlecht.
Ja, ich weiß, aber was soll das sozusagen heißen?
Moment, wo ist eigentlich Pina?
Pina, bitte sofort in mein Büro!
Let's unpack Beyza's blunt assessment and all the everyday ways Thorsten asks 'what do you mean by that?'
Die Zahlen sehen ja nicht so gut aus, oder?

'The numbers don't look so good, do they?' Saying something 'looks good' or 'not so good' uses a split-apart expression built from 'see' and 'out' at the end. Tacking the word for 'or?' onto the close turns any statement into 'don't they?' or 'right?'.
Wie meinst du das jetzt?

'What do you mean by that now?' Watch how English 'what do you mean?' starts with the word for 'how' rather than 'what' in German — literally 'how mean you that now?'. That single swap will make your questions sound instantly natural.
Ja, aber was heißt das genau?
'Yes, right, what does that mean exactly?' When asking what a word, sign, or remark means, German reaches for the same action word used to state a name — literally 'what is that called exactly?'.
Was heißt das wohl? Die Zahlen sind einfach schlecht.

'What do you think it means? The numbers are simply bad.' Slipping that little middle word in after 'what means that' adds dry irony — 'what do you suppose it means?' — before Beyza spells it out with the plain word for 'simply'.
Ja, ich weiß, aber was soll das sozusagen heißen?

'Yes, I know, only what is that supposed to mean, so to speak?' Pairing 'should' with 'mean' at the end creates a classic reusable chunk: 'what is that supposed to mean?', padded out with Thorsten's nervous 'so to speak'.
Pina, bitte sofort in mein Büro!

'Pina, to my office right away, please!' Announcements over a shop loudspeaker often drop the action word completely: literally 'into my office' says everything needed in three brisk words. Now let's listen to the whole office confrontation again.
So, schön, dass du da bist!
Die Zahlen sehen ja nicht so gut aus, oder?
Wie meinst du das jetzt?
Wie meine ich das? Also, die Zahlen sehen nicht so gut aus.
Ja, aber was heißt das genau?
Was heißt das wohl? Die Zahlen sind einfach schlecht.
Ja, ich weiß, aber was soll das sozusagen heißen?
Moment, wo ist eigentlich Pina?
Pina, bitte sofort in mein Büro!

Whenever a real business question lands on his desk, Thorsten hits the intercom button for Pina. You have practised saying how things look, asking what someone means, asking what something is supposed to mean, and calling a colleague into an office. Until next time!
Bis später!
